 Kyshawn George and the Wizards fell apart in the fourth quarter against a shorthanded Pacers team. Michael Hickey / Getty Images 
 By Josh Robbins Nov. 12, 2026 6:00 am EST Updated Share article 44 INDIANAPOLIS — If you have ever peeled garlic and minced the cloves with a knife and your bare hands, you know that the smell can linger no matter how thoroughly you try to wash it away with soap and water.
 The same goes for the residue of tanking. The stench takes time to scrub off.
 After 12 games this season, we can surmise that tanking has had an enduring negative impact on the young Washington Wizards players who endured loss after loss after loss the previous few years. Bub Carrington, Tre Johnson, Kyshawn George, Bilal Coulibaly and Alex Sarr displayed their bad on-court habits Wednesday night during a crucial stretch against the Indiana Pacers, leading to the Wizards’ fifth consecutive defeat, a 114-101 loss at Gainbridge Fieldhouse.
 Advertisement
 With the score tied 77-77, Wizards coach Brian Keefe opened the fourth quarter with a lineup of those five players. A parade of mistakes followed. On defense, they left a good 3-point shooter wide open, allowed a drive to the basket by Pascal Siakam that led to a corner 3, and failed to navigate the Pacers’ screens. On offense, they committed two turnovers and took a contested 3-pointer as their ball and player movement slowed to a crawl. Because of those errors, Indiana scored 12 consecutive points over a two-minute, 12-second stretch and broke the game open.
 “I thought the difference in the game was we got stagnant there to start the fourth quarter,” Keefe said. “The ball movement that we had in the second quarter wasn’t there. They obviously went on a run. Our defense was not tied together as much as I would have liked.”
 Wizards officials entered this season — their most highly anticipated since the heyday of John Wall and Bradley Beal — preaching patience. Rather than saying the goal was to reach the postseason, Monumental Basketball president Michael Winger and general manager Will Dawkins spoke of giving their homegrown players more opportunities to play in close games and to learn from those experiences. That’s why, Winger and Dawkins have said, they traded for former All-Stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis: to help the youngsters grow.

 In the Wizards organization alone, Dybantsa has three people who know exactly what it feels like to be the draft’s top pick
 Wednesday night provided one of those experiences. Keefe said afterward that his players will learn from their mistakes.
 At the same time, though, the Pacers’ decisive run felt like so many other ones against the Wizards over the last few years, like a case of déjà vu. Coulibaly joined the team as a rookie through a draft-night trade in 2023. Sarr, Carrington and George arrived on draft night in 2024. The Wizards selected Johnson sixth in 2025.
 Advertisement
 No one expected this season would be easy. Indeed, rival talent evaluators warned that making the transition from tanking to trying to win typically involves significant growing pains.
 Wednesday’s loss still stung. The Pacers played without injured star point guard Tyrese Haliburton and entered the night having lost seven of their last eight games. You could argue that, with Davis, Young and No. 1 draft pick AJ Dybantsa in the fold, along with their youthful nucleus, the Wizards had more healthy talent than the Pacers.
 One of the benefits of the Wizards’ tanking over the previous three seasons was that young players received more minutes than if they had been drafted by competitive teams. All of that playing time was supposed to hasten their development.
 Perhaps all of those minutes helped players build individual skills, but they did not teach the youngsters how to win. Those lessons are supposed to ramp up this season.
 It still felt jarring to see the Carrington, Johnson, George, Coulibaly and Sarr lineup struggle when it mattered most. The same quintet had performed well to begin the second quarter, outscoring Indiana 14-7 over a 5:33 stretch.
 There is a difference, though, between early second-quarter minutes and early fourth-quarter minutes.
 “We didn’t get stops,” George said. “We didn’t value each possession as we should have, and that’s how they kind of pulled away.”
 The Wizards have now lost five in a row. (Michael Conroy / Associated Press) The entire team seems to be struggling on offense these days. To call the offense merely “clunky” on Wednesday night would have been an understatement. Even with Young and Davis on the floor, the ball and player movement were at times almost nonexistent. Through the first three quarters, Washington totaled only eight assists on 29 made baskets.
 On one hand, the offense’s struggles are understandable. Washington is integrating three high-usage players — Davis, Young and Dybantsa — into a team that moved the ball better last season, even though the offense finished next to last in the NBA in points per possession.
 Advertisement
 On the other hand, those additions cannot fully explain why so many Wizards seem so slow to both make decisions with the ball and begin actions. Davis, Young and Dybantsa cannot be blamed for the lack of ball movement to begin the fourth quarter. They were not on the floor.
 “We’ve got to figure this out,” Coulibaly said. “We’ve got to work on that and get better.”
 The 2026-27 Wizards are a team marked by dramatic changes. The returning players have seen their spots in the offensive pecking order change, and, in some cases, their minutes reduced.
 The largest change of all is that Washington is trying to win, and that requires an adjustment for the likes of Carrington, Johnson, George, Coulibaly and Sarr, who perhaps had grown too tolerant of losing.
 Young has struggled, too. During the losing streak, he has averaged 16 points, 6 assists and 3.4 turnovers per game while shooting 41 percent from the field.
 Young had pointed the finger at himself for his poor performances during Friday’s loss in Atlanta and Saturday’s defeat in Oklahoma City. On Wednesday, he added that the entire offense needs to gain more fluidity and rhythm.
 “We’ve got a lot of talented young guys that obviously need the ball in their hands to score, and I think sometimes they try to go make a play, and it’s not selfishly,” Young said. “But they just try to go and make a play and that’s what we need.
 “We need guys to be aggressive but, at the same time, continue to make the right plays. If somebody’s open, find him. Sometimes make a good-to-great pass (to turn down a good shot in search of a great shot), and that could be the best pass and best play available. So when we get there, we’ll become a better offensive team.”

 Every team has at least one win now, so let's say something nice about each squad.
 Keefe called a timeout after a fast-break dunk by Jalen Slawson extended Indiana’s run to 12-0 to begin the fourth quarter, and subbed Davis, Young and Dybantsa back into the game for Sarr, Carrington and Coulibaly.
 Advertisement
 On the Pacers’ next possession, point guard Andrew Nembhard dribbled the ball near the left break of the 3-point arc with Young guarding him and the shot clock down to five seconds. Young turned to crew chief Tyler Ford to complain about something, and Nembhard dribbled forward a few steps, elevated from the free-throw line and sank a jumper, extending the Pacers’ lead to 91-77.
 Later, in the Wizards’ locker room, Young explained that Nembhard should have been whistled for a double-dribble.
 Maybe so, but the sequence was emblematic of the Wizards’ night as a whole: A host of bad habits they needs to unlearn.
